summary.overview: Partitioning (sharding) splits a dataset that is too large or too hot for one machine across many nodes, each holding a disjoint subset of the data. The chapter is really about the decisions this forces: how to assign records to partitions (key range vs hash), how to handle secondary indexes and skewed hot keys, how to rebalance when nodes join or leave, and how clients find the partition holding their data. It matters because partitioning is the core scaling technique behind nearly every distributed database, and its trade-offs appear constantly in system design interviews.

sections.heading: Partitioning and Replication
takeaways: Replication mainly buys availability and lower latency; partitioning mainly buys scalability. They solve different problems, so production systems almost always use both.
The two choices are largely independent: a node can hold several partitions and typically acts as leader for some partitions and follower for others.

Each record belongs to exactly one partition, and each partition behaves like a small database of its own. Different systems call partitions shards (MongoDB, Elasticsearch), regions (HBase), tablets (Bigtable), vnodes (Cassandra, Riak), or vBuckets (Couchbase).

sections.heading: Partitioning of Key-Value Data
takeaways: Key-range partitioning assigns contiguous key ranges to partitions, which makes range scans efficient but risks uneven partitions and hot spots when data or traffic is skewed.
Hash partitioning applies a hash function to the key, spreading data and load evenly, but it destroys key order so range queries must fan out to all partitions.
Skewed workloads create hot keys (e.g., a celebrity's data); the fix is to split the hot key into several subkeys (e.g., append a random suffix), spread the writes, and combine the parts on read.
A common compromise partitions on part of a compound key, keeping related records together for locality while spreading load better than pure key-range partitioning.

sections.heading: Partitioning and Secondary Indexes
takeaways: With document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes, each partition indexes only its own documents: writes stay in one partition, but any query on the index must scatter-gather across all partitions.

With term-partitioned (global) secondary indexes, the index itself is partitioned by the indexed terms: a query touches one partition, but writing one document can require updates in many partitions, creating cross-partition consistency challenges.

Local document-partitioned indexes are the common default (MongoDB, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, Riak); global term-partitioned indexes appear in systems like DynamoDB, where their writes are typically asynchronous.

sections.heading: Rebalancing Partitions
takeaways: Rebalancing (moving partitions when nodes join, leave, or fill up) must keep serving reads and writes, move as little data as necessary, and leave load fairly shared afterward.
The naive approach, hash mod N, is a trap: changing the number of nodes remaps nearly every key, forcing almost all data to move.

Fixed number of partitions (Riak, Elasticsearch, Couchbase): create far more partitions than nodes and rebalance by moving whole partitions; simple, but the partition count is hard to change once set.

Dynamic partitioning (HBase, MongoDB): split a partition when it grows past a threshold (and merge tiny ones); adapts to data size, but a small new dataset starts with few partitions unless you pre-split.
Proportional partitioning with consistent hashing (Cassandra): boundaries are fixed random points on a ring, so a joining node takes over ranges from its neighbors and only nearby data moves.

sections.heading: Request Routing
takeaways: Requests can be routed by sending to any node and letting it forward, by a dedicated routing tier, or by a partition-aware client; analytic (MPP) databases additionally run a single query in parallel across partitions and merge the results.
Whoever routes must learn partition-to-node assignments, via a coordination service like ZooKeeper (HBase, Solr), a gossip protocol between nodes (Cassandra), or a client-kept mapping.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: Partitioning exists for scale: datasets or throughputs too big for one machine. It is normally combined with replication so the system also survives node failures.
Designing a partitioned system means choosing a partition scheme, handling skew and hot keys, picking a secondary-index strategy, planning rebalancing, and deciding how requests are routed.
